segments.content:
Chapter 266 (0263) Chen Ten Billion and Successology

Just as universities across the country were starting their new semester, New Oriental was listed on the New York Stock Exchange.

Chen Guiliang held last semester's College English textbook, pretending to review for his makeup exam while wondering if he should sign up for a class at New Oriental.

This semester, he had to pass the Level 4 English exam, no matter what!

Whether he could get his graduation certificate was another matter; the main thing was, it would be too damn embarrassing if word got out.

"Sigh, how did I ever manage to study English in my third year of high school? I even memorized 25 new words a day," Chen Guiliang lamented.

After looking at vocabulary for a while, Chen Guiliang tossed the English book aside.

He picked up a pen and paper and started writing back to the underprivileged children he sponsored last year, while also writing letters to the children he was sponsoring this year.

Between the two groups, he was sponsoring 13 children in total.

They were all excellent students from poor families, and it didn't cost much to sponsor one.

In this day and age, sponsorships like this were still needed, but in another ten-plus years, they probably wouldn't be. As long as someone was willing to study, they definitely wouldn't have to worry about tuition fees.

But for now, there were genuinely many students who dropped out because they couldn't afford it.

He rather admired Senior Min Wenyu, who went to teach in the mountains every summer. If it were him, Chen Guiliang knew he wouldn't have that kind of perseverance.

"Chen Guiliang, you still haven't chosen your courses for the academic year?" The group leader for the Yuanpei Program sent him a text.

Senior Long Xiang had already graduated and been admitted to graduate school, so Chen Guiliang no longer had an advisor.

He was a junior now, so he didn't need one anyway.

Thus, the eleven students under their mentor elected a group leader to pass on information.

Chen Guiliang replied: "I've chosen them. I'll email them to you."

"You haven't decided on a major yet?"

"I'll just drift for now. I'm not in a hurry to pick a major."

"You're amazing. Not worried at all."

Students could declare their majors in the second semester of their sophomore year, but half the students in the Yuanpei Program hadn't.

Now, in the first semester of their junior year, his classmates were starting to panic. For the past few days, everyone had been discussing it in the campus network groups, comparing notes to see what major would be suitable.

Chen Guiliang continued to be a free agent.

Moreover, he had already completed all the required courses for freshman and sophomore year. He had even more freedom this semester and could choose whatever he wanted.

History direction: *History of Ancient Chinese Political Systems*, *History of Modern Chinese Thought*.

Literature direction: *Research on Ancient Novels*.

Philosophy direction: *History of Modern Western Philosophy*, *Introduction to Phenomenology*, *Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism*.

Sociology direction: *History of Chinese Social Thought*, *Economic Sociology*.

Political Science direction: *History of Western Political Thought*, *Theory of International Politics*.

Economics direction: Continuing and delving deeper into the management-related courses from last year. He also chose *Topics in the Chinese Economy* by that professor who liked to play basketball and swim.

He had signed up for the most courses in economics and philosophy.

"Mr. Chen, hello. We've arrived at the South Gate of Peking University," Yang Lan called to say.

Chen Guiliang said, "Wait a moment, I'll come get you. By the way, just call me Xiao Chen."

"That won't do, we should still use a formal address," Yang Lan said. "Tell me your dormitory building number."

"Alright, wait for me downstairs. I'll go talk to the dorm manager auntie and the custodian on duty, otherwise you won't be able to get in..."

Every time Yang Lan did an interview, she would go to the interviewee's workplace or living space, never minding how tiring it was. Chen Guiliang seriously suspected it was because she didn't have a proper studio.

She ran her own private television station. *The Yang Lan Interviews* would premiere on her own station before being sold for rebroadcast to channels like Dragon TV.

After Chen Guiliang settled things with the dorm management, he found Yang Lan's team being watched by a few students.

"Ms. Yang, hello," Chen Guiliang also used a more formal address.

Yang Lan said, "Let's go up."

Chen Guiliang voiced his opinion again: "You have cameras, lights, and sound equipment. There's simply no space for all that in the dorm room."

"We can film in the hallway outside your room. The audience will definitely be interested in that kind of interview setting," Yang Lan explained the effect she wanted for the show. Then she added with a smile, "After the interview, we'll also need to go to your two companies to shoot some footage."

Chen Guiliang could only agree.

After going upstairs, he visited every room on the floor to let them know he might be blocking the hallway and to ask for their understanding.

The students were all very easygoing. While Yang Lan's team was adjusting the lights and sound, they all came over to watch the excitement and chat.

Yang Lan was very approachable. While talking with the students, she said to the cameraman, "Get some shots of the dorm room and the hallway, just use natural light. Show his usual living environment."

She handed Chen Guiliang the interview script. "Mr. Chen, you can take a look first. If there are any topics you don't want to discuss, I can change them on the spot."

Chen Guiliang glanced at it. "We can talk about anything."

Once all the equipment was set up, the students very considerately dispersed.

Yang Lan told them, "As long as you're quiet, you can pass through freely. It doesn't matter if you accidentally get in the shot."

She wanted to make a very special episode because this episode's guest was very special.

The interview began, but not according to the script. From the very first question, it was all improvised.

And it continued to be improvised all the way through!

The script was practically a useless piece of paper.

Yang Lan: "I remember the old-style student dorms used to have a common area on each floor for watching TV or for studying and socializing. How come this building doesn't have one?"

Chen Guiliang: "Most of the old buildings at Peking University do, but this building is especially old. You can't even find a faucet in the dorm rooms."

Yang Lan: "Your companies are very successful now. Do you find the living conditions here harsh? Have you ever thought about renting an apartment or buying a house off-campus?"

Chen Guiliang: "I'm afraid if I lived off-campus, I'd stop coming to class altogether. I don't have much perseverance, so I need an environment to force me. As for the harsh conditions, everyone else can live here, so why can't I?"

Yang Lan: "You were a left-behind child. Was it always this harsh growing up?"

Chen Guiliang: "It was alright."

Yang Lan: "You don't seem to want to talk about that. Are you avoiding your past?"

Chen Guiliang: "There have been too many reports about it. Bringing it up every time feels like it would annoy people. It feels like I'm trying to sell a sob story."

Yang Lan: "A background like that can win sympathy and attention. Some people treat it as a form of capital."

Chen Guiliang: "Very few people are purely virtuous. If you constantly sell a sob story to attract attention, the day some dirt on you gets dug up, the public backlash will be severe."

Yang Lan: "Do you have dirt on you too?"

Chen Guiliang: "I do, but it's not too bad, the kind that wouldn't matter if it was made public. It's possible I'll make mistakes in the future too. Who can say for sure?"

Yang Lan: "You're very rational."

Chen Guiliang: "I'm a sentimental person, and I'm often very impulsive. But I try my best to exercise restraint. I signed up for *Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism* this semester. Haha, maybe I can learn some self-cultivation techniques."

Yang Lan: "It seems Yuanpei Program students can choose their courses freely. Which ones did you pick?"

Chen Guiliang: "This semester I chose..."

Chen Guiliang: "My course load is actually quite lazy. Guo Feng, a shareholder at ByteDance, is the one who chooses courses like a beast. At first, he majored in biology, but he ended up taking a bunch of courses on things like ancient architecture restoration. After we started the company together and he became responsible for ByteDance's tech, he finally switched his major to computer science."

Yang Lan: "A very interesting person. I'll have to interview him next time. How do you think the freedom of the Yuanpei Program has influenced your growth and career?"

Chen Guiliang: "It's convenient for skipping class. For Yuanpei students, the professors don't take attendance. Because sometimes if you don't show up for a class, it's because of a schedule conflict with another course you signed up for. Even final exams can conflict, forcing the professor to create a makeup exam paper."

Yang Lan: "What a novel educational model. Even exams can have conflicts. So you often skip class to handle business at your company?"

Chen Guiliang: "Yes. It can't be helped. The number of employees at ByteDance has surpassed 200, and Game Science has over 160. I have to be responsible for their livelihoods, and I also have to be responsible to the investors."

Yang Lan: "So, you said earlier you were afraid you'd stop coming to school altogether. Is it because you're too busy with work and writing?"

Chen Guiliang: "It's much more relaxed now. The companies are running normally, and the management can handle most of the affairs. It was only hectic when I was first starting out. Thinking back now, I don't even know how I got through it."

Yang Lan: "I heard that Xiaonei has surpassed ten million users?"

Chen Guiliang: "That's right, and most of them are university students. I estimate that nearly half of all undergraduate and junior college students in the country are using our Xiaonei."

Yang Lan: "That's a shocking statistic. You control the online social lives of half the university students in the country."

Chen Guiliang: "I wouldn't call it controlling. I'd say we're providing an online social platform for students. Hainei, which is a platform for everyone, surpassed ten million registered users two months ago. Many celebrities have also chosen to interact with everyone on our website."

Yang Lan: "You haven't even graduated, yet you've built such a huge business. Has your mentality changed at all?"

Chen Guiliang: "It'd be a lie to say it hasn't. Sometimes I feel like I'm the bee's knees. Heaven is number one, Earth is number two, and I'm number three. That's a bad mentality. It's easy to become detached from the masses, to become arrogant and clueless."

Yang Lan: "How do you adjust?"

Chen Guiliang: "*Shèn dú*."

Yang Lan: "Hmm?"

Chen Guiliang: "It means to be strict with yourself and to engage in self-reflection even when no one is supervising you. I'm not saying I want to become some kind of saint, but everyone makes mistakes every day. Recognizing those mistakes and trying to correct them is how you constantly improve yourself."

Yang Lan: "I've learned a new term. You seem more like a man of culture than a businessman, which is evident from your book, *Those Things About the Ming Dynasty*."

Chen Guiliang: "It's alright. I have many professors who help me check it over to avoid making factual errors as much as possible."

Yang Lan: "The fourth and fifth volumes of your *Those Things About the Ming Dynasty* recently climbed to second place on the bestseller list."

Chen Guiliang: "What book is number one?"

Yang Lan: "*The World Is Flat*, a foreign business management book."

Chen Guiliang: "Then I have no complaints. That one sells well all over the world."

Yang Lan: "In third place is *Analyzing the Three Kingdoms*. As a fellow work of popular history, how would you comment on *Analyzing the Three Kingdoms*?"

Chen Guiliang: "I'd rather not comment."

Yang Lan: "Why is that?"

Chen Guiliang: "Professor Yi is a professor in the Chinese Department, not the History Department. I'll reserve my opinion."

Yang Lan: "The fourth and fifth places are Guo Xiaosi's *Cry Me a Sad River* and Han Han's *A Fortress Besieged*. You all came from the New Concept Writing Competition, and they've even helped promote your book on their blogs. Are you still in touch?"

Chen Guiliang: "That's a secret."

Yang Lan: "Will you continue to maintain your triple identity as a student, author, and businessman in the future? Have you considered taking a leave of absence from school?"

Chen Guiliang: "As long as Peking University doesn't expel me, I'll shamelessly stick around. After I finish *Those Things About the Ming Dynasty*, I don't plan to write any more books, at least not another long series like this. This book is projected to be eight or nine volumes, and researching for it is absolutely exhausting."

They talked for several tens of minutes, and there was no telling how Yang Lan would edit it in the end.

She also took her team to film a bit at Chen Guiliang's companies.

Later on, the CCTV program *Dialogue*, which was billed as a high-end talk show, was at this time actually taking a more populist approach. The general public loved watching celebrities clash on *Dialogue*.

*Behind the Headlines* and *The Yang Lan Interviews*, on the other hand, targeted a more mid-to-high-end audience and were especially popular among white-collar workers and students. In truth, the content of their conversations was still mostly casual chat.

That episode of *Behind the Headlines* had already aired. The TV ratings were average, but it was very popular online. The number of pirated downloads and online streams was exceptionally high.

When *The Yang Lan Interviews* aired, the effect would certainly be better, since it had a platform like Dragon TV.

It could boost his prestige.

What Chen Guiliang didn't expect was that after his long chat with Yang Lan, the two words that ended up catching on were "*shèn dú*."

Because many entrepreneurs, executives, and white-collar workers watched the show, they felt that "*shèn dú*" had a particularly classy ring to it. After inquiring and learning the origin of the term, they started using it as a catchphrase.

Some even commissioned calligraphers to write out the words "*shèn dú*" to hang in their offices.

Entrepreneurs followed trends too. One moment they were chasing the "wolf culture" of *Wolf Totem*, the next they were chasing Wang Yangming's "School of the Mind," and later they would all flock to chase Liu Cixin's *The Three-Body Problem*.

Coincidentally, Yu Dan was very popular at this time, so *The Analects* and the like could be used to seem sophisticated.

Chen Guiliang's mention of "*shèn dú*" caught the wave of Professor Yu's Confucian trend and inexplicably became popular in certain circles.

This was especially true for those entrepreneurs who came from humble beginnings, lacked much culture, and wanted to package themselves as cultured individuals!

Since the entrepreneurs liked it, the "masters" of successology naturally had to adopt it too. As it happened, Chen Guiliang was quite successful and could serve as a real-life case study for successology.

Damn, just imagine the scene:

In a grand-looking hall, a successology master stands on stage in a suit and tie, facing a crowd of adults who have paid to attend the seminar.

The speakers play "The Sun Is Always After the Rain" or "A True Hero" as the master tells Chen Guiliang's inspirational start-up story, peddling the currently fashionable Confucian self-cultivation knowledge. He spouts "*shèn dú*" one moment and "*The Analects*' way of navigating the world" the next...

They'd talk you into a daze.

(End of this chapter)
